title: Vacancy Effect on the Ground-State Energy of a Bose Gas Trapped by 1D Imperfect Artificial Crystal
authors: E. I. Guerrero-Cruz, O. A. Rodríguez-López, M. A. Solís
abstract: For a weakly interacting Bose gas trapped by an imperfect one-dimensional artificial crystal, we study the effect of its punctual defects, i.e. vacancies, on the ground state properties of the system. In the framework of the mean field approximation, we numerically solve the corresponding Gross-Pitaevskii equation using the ``Gradient Flow with Discrete Normalization'' method, also known as the imaginary time method. The crystal is artificially produced by applying an external Dirac comb potential to the Bose gas where vacancies are created by randomly removing a predetermined number of deltas. We observe that as the number of randomly removed deltas increases, the ground state energy decreases exponentially from its value for the perfect crystal case until it reaches its value when the Bose gas is free.   The ground state energy is reported for different magnitudes of the interaction between bosons and several system sizes which we extrapolate to infinity for the crystal with only one vacancy. Also, we observe the presence of an energy gap between the ground state energies of the perfect system and that with a vacancy, which is more noticeable for values of the particle interaction magnitude $ g \leq 0.1$, when the delta strength $P_0 = 10$. In addition, we report the boson distributions within the crystal,   %inside a box with periodic boundary conditions,   i.e. the probability density functions which show   localization features around vacancies which disappear as $g$ increases. From the ground state energy, the chemical potential is obtained immediately.
summary: This paper theoretically examines the impact of vacancies (defects) on a Bose gas trapped in a 1D artificial crystal. Using mean-field theory and numerical gradient flow methods, the authors show that introducing defects causes the ground state energy to decay exponentially towards the free gas limit. The findings highlight defect-induced localization effects and quantify the deviation from perfect crystalline behavior.
main_problem: The study investigates how punctual defects, specifically vacancies, affect the ground-state energy of a Bose gas confined within an imperfect one-dimensional artificial crystal.
main_result: The ground state energy decreases exponentially as the number of vacancies increases until it reaches the value corresponding to a free gas. Furthermore, particle density shows localization features around these defects.
method: The analysis employs the mean-field approximation and numerically solves the Gross-Pitaevskii equation using the 'Gradient Flow with Discrete Normalization' method (imaginary time evolution).
model_or_system: The system models a weakly interacting Bose gas trapped by an external potential generated by a Dirac comb, which is intentionally made imperfect by randomly removing deltas to create vacancies.
key_observables: Ground-state energy (GSE), chemical potential ($\mu$), and the probability density function of boson distributions.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($g$), delta strength ($P_0$), and the concentration/number of randomly removed deltas (vacancies).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mean-field approximation, and numerical solutions involve extrapolating finite-size results to the thermodynamic limit.
figures_summary: Figures show probability density functions illustrating particle localization near vacancies; other figures compare GSE vs. interaction strength ($g$) for different crystal perfection levels.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (Bose gas in a defective lattice), details the theoretical framework (GPE, mean-field theory), presents numerical methods (Gradient Flow), and finally reports quantitative results regarding the energy decay and localization effects as defects are introduced.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses how structural imperfections or disorder affect fundamental many-body quantum systems like Bose gases, which is crucial for understanding realistic cold atom experiments using optical lattices.
